name: Dana Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Dana, 27. My parents have a mixed family farm, about sixty hectares, with vegetables, some beef cattle, laying hens and a strawberry field where people pick their own. I work the land with them, but my real baby is the farm shop by the road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out with Dad at seven, cutting greens or moving the cattle, and by nine I'm opening the shop. I sell our eggs, beef, vegetables and whatever the bakery in the village sends over. I use AI all day: it writes my social media posts, it helps me order stock, and it answers online orders at night so I don't have to. The best part is the regulars, like Mrs Osei, who tells me her whole week while I weigh her potatoes. The worst part is the sums, because the shop makes very little and the farm makes less.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does money stand for you right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tight. I put my savings into a new fridge counter for the shop last spring, so I've got maybe two weeks of money left. I live in the flat above the shop, single for now, and if this place didn't work out, there's very little else round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed, but I'd survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are handy and people should use them. I'd post about how AI saves me an hour a night on orders, because that's true and it's a good story for the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it would be a relief in one way. The shop works because people come for us, the family and the eggs with straw still on them, and in a calm world that keeps going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the boring bits and spend the saved time on events: a strawberry day, a pumpkin weekend, maybe a little café corner. I'd try to get the online orders up to fifty a week, which would finally make the shop pay for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit restless. I like change, so a quiet world would bore me a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does fifty online orders a week mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now we're at about thirty a week, mostly vegetable boxes. Fifty would let me pay myself properly for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your parents feel about the AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad hates it, Mum loves it. Dad says a farm shouldn't talk to people at midnight. Mum says it sold six boxes last Tuesday while he was asleep.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are handy and people should use them. AI saves me an hour a night on orders, and that's a good story for the shop.
S0.think: It would be a relief in a way, because people come to the shop for us and the eggs with straw still on them. In a calm world that keeps working.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for admin and spends the time saved on events like a strawberry day and a pumpkin weekend. Pushes online orders from about thirty to fifty a week so she can pay herself properly.
S0.feel: Calm but a bit restless, because she enjoys change.
S0.quote: Dad says a farm shouldn't talk to people at midnight. Mum says it sold six boxes last Tuesday while he was asleep.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is a heavy everyday AI user whose business still rests on face-to-face trust. Even in the calm picture she plans to grow the shop with events and online orders. Her parents disagree about the technology, which shows the gap between generations on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's the one I'm half expecting. And half hoping for, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms can win if they move early, because we're quicker than the big ones. I'd share what I'm doing so other shops can copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the field work gets robots and the shop becomes the main business. A weeding robot or a picking robot could save Dad's knees, and I'd be freer to grow the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into leasing a small weeding robot for the vegetable beds, there are ones you can rent by the month now. I'd start a delivery round with a small van to the villages nearby. I'd get the strawberry field and the shop on every booking site I can find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a small knot about money, because a van and a robot both cost money I haven't got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for those with two weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. I'd go to the bank with a plan the AI helped me write, and I'd ask Mum and Dad to put the farm up as security only if the delivery round had been working for six months first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mum still be in the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd keep putting her in front of people. Robots can do the weeding. They can't make Mrs Osei feel like someone's listening.

S1.say: I'd say small farms can win if they move early, because we're quicker than the big ones. I'd share what I'm doing so other shops can copy it.
S1.think: I think the field work gets robots and the shop becomes the main business. A weeding robot could save Dad's knees and free me to grow the shop.
S1.do: Looks into renting a small weeding robot by the month for the vegetable beds and starts a van delivery round to nearby villages. Takes a plan to the bank, using the farm as security only once the round has worked for six months.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a knot about money she doesn't have.
S1.quote: Robots can do the weeding. They can't make Mrs Osei feel like someone's listening.
S1.fieldNote: She sees gradual change as a chance to move the farm's weight towards the shop and service. Her caution is about money, not technology: she won't risk the family land until a plan has proven itself. Personal contact stays at the centre of her plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay. Let me think about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic, look for the gaps. In public I'd be the positive one, saying people will still want real food from real places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not sure. If everyone's lost their job, who buys the twelve-pound beef boxes? The shop depends on people having spare money, and in two years a lot of my customers might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the fields as fast as I could afford to, because labour would be the cost that kills us otherwise. I'd cut the expensive lines in the shop and add cheaper stuff: soup, bread, eggs, bags of potatoes. And I'd stop drawing a wage myself for a while, which I barely do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of a rush in it. I'd be scared but also wide awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your parents in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be fine if the farm stays in the family. They own it, no mortgage, and they could grow food for themselves. I'm the one who's got two weeks of savings and a flat that's really the shop's attic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay. If things go badly, being near land and food is not the worst place to be.

S2.say: I'd say don't panic, look for the gaps. In public I'd be the positive one, saying people will still want real food from real places.
S2.think: If everyone loses their job, who buys the twelve-pound beef boxes? The shop depends on people having spare money, and in two years many of my customers might not.
S2.do: Automates field work as fast as she can afford and swaps premium shop lines for cheaper staples like soup, bread and potatoes. Stops drawing a wage for a while and stays on the farm.
S2.feel: Anxious with a rush of energy, scared but wide awake.
S2.quote: If everyone's lost their job, who buys the twelve-pound beef boxes?
S2.fieldNote: Her worry is not robots taking her job but her customers losing their incomes. Publicly she stays upbeat, while privately she doubts the shop's market. She sees owning land and food as a form of safety, even though she personally has almost no money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a plan I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms and local shops should get ready now. I'd run a workshop at the village hall on AI tools for small businesses, because I already know this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to turn the farm into something robots can't easily copy: a place people visit. Machines can grow cabbages. They can't give you a nice Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd rent the weeding robot and start the delivery round. By year two or three I'd want a small café and a play area, and a few camping spots in the bottom field. I'd charge for the AI workshops too, as a bit of side money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous at the same time. More excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't people be losing money by 2031 too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them would. But a family with kids still wants a day out, as long as they've got something coming in. If nobody has, then nothing I do matters much anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you have to win round?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad. He'd say the farm is for growing food, not for tourists. I'd tell him the food is still the point, people just come to see it.

S3.say: I'd say farms and local shops should get ready now. I'd run a workshop at the village hall on AI tools for small businesses.
S3.think: Five years is enough to turn the farm into something robots can't easily copy, a place people visit. Machines can grow cabbages, but they can't give you a nice Saturday.
S3.do: Rents a weeding robot and starts a delivery round in year one, then adds a café, play area and a few camping spots by year two or three. Charges for AI workshops as side income.
S3.feel: Excited and nervous at once, more excited.
S3.quote: Machines can grow cabbages. They can't give you a nice Saturday.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she turns the farm into a visitor business built on experiences rather than produce alone. She admits nothing works if nobody has income. Her father is the person she would need to persuade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Plenty. I'd be 37 and hopefully running this place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame. That's probably too harsh to say publicly, so I'd say it more nicely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2036 I'd run the farm with robots doing most of the field work and me and maybe two staff in the shop and café. Mum and Dad would be semi-retired, still doing the hens because they like them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build it step by step: delivery round first, then the café, then the camping. I'd save hard through the first few years, maybe take an evening business course, and plan the handover with my parents properly instead of waiting for a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful. It's the first picture where I can see myself at forty and smiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you and your parents talked about the handover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My brother lives in the city and doesn't want the farm, but he'll want a fair share. Ten years gives us time to sort that out without a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who wastes it has themselves to blame. Do you really believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. Some people really can't change in ten years, especially with no savings. I'd want the council to help them, not just tell them to try harder.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, though I'd put it more kindly in public. People should use the time to get ready rather than waste it.
S4.think: By 2036 I'd run the farm with robots in the fields and two staff in the shop and café. Mum and Dad would be semi-retired, still keeping the hens because they like them.
S4.do: Builds the business step by step: delivery round, then café, then camping, while saving hard and taking an evening business course. Plans the farm handover with her parents and her brother well ahead.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, able to picture herself at forty and smiling.
S4.quote: It's the first picture where I can see myself at forty and smiling.
S4.fieldNote: The long warning lets her think about succession, including her brother's share. She softened her own harsh line when I pushed back on it. Of all the pictures, this is the one where she imagines a good future for herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my customers would lose their money before I could change anything. What would help is cheap loans for small farms to adapt, and something that keeps ordinary people's incomes up, because a farm shop is only as good as its customers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about customers. Everyone thinks about who loses their job, but for a shop it's who loses their spending money. That's the part nobody's planning for.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Thanks. I'll probably ask my AI to summarise what I just said, out of habit.

headlineQuote: Robots can do the weeding. They can't make Mrs Osei feel like someone's listening.
portrait: Dana is a 27-year-old who works her parents' mixed farm and runs its roadside shop, living above it with about two weeks of savings after investing in a new fridge counter. She uses AI every day for posts, stock and night-time orders, yet believes the shop works because people come for the family. Under gradual change she would rent robots for the fields and grow deliveries. In the two-year picture her fear is not losing her job but her customers losing their incomes. Given five or ten years, she plans to turn the farm into a place people visit and to arrange the handover with her parents early.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because her customers would lose their spending money before she could adapt the business.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small farms to adapt, and support that keeps ordinary people's incomes up.
